guide.title: Period 4 (1800–1848): review guide
guide.intro: Between 1800 and 1848 the young republic expanded its territory, its economy, and its democracy, while arguments over federal power, slavery, and reform deepened. Causation is the period's key reasoning skill.

sections.title: Parties, federal power, and foreign policy
body: Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans took power in 1800; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) doubled the nation's size. Chief Justice John Marshall's Supreme Court strengthened federal power (Marbury v. Madison, 1803; McCulloch v. Maryland, 1819). The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine (1823) asserted American independence in foreign affairs.

Regional interests clashed over tariffs, internal improvements, and slavery: the Missouri Compromise (1820) balanced slave and free states; the Nullification Crisis (1832) pitted South Carolina against federal tariffs; Andrew Jackson vetoed the Second Bank of the United States and backed Indian removal even after Worcester v. Georgia (1832).
points: The second party system: Democrats vs. Whigs.
Debates over federal power ran through the bank, tariffs, and removal.

sections.title: The Market Revolution and the South
body: Canals (the Erie Canal, 1825), steamboats, and early railroads linked farms to distant markets. Textile mills such as those at Lowell, Massachusetts, hired young women and later immigrants; factory work changed family life and gave rise to a growing middle class and new class divisions.

In the South, the cotton gin (1793) and global demand for cotton spread plantation slavery westward, making the South more dependent on enslaved labor and on Northern and British markets. Causation: improved transportation and new technology produced regional specialization.
points: Regional economies: Northern manufacturing, Western farming, Southern cotton.
Cotton's expansion drove both the domestic slave trade and pressure on American Indian lands.

sections.title: Democracy, religion, reform, and African Americans
body: Most states dropped property requirements for white male voting, expanding democracy for some while free Black men often lost the vote. The Second Great Awakening's revivals stressed individual choice and inspired reform movements: temperance, prison and asylum reform (Dorothea Dix), public education, abolition, and women's rights (Seneca Falls, 1848).

Abolitionists such as William Lloyd Garrison demanded immediate emancipation; free and enslaved African Americans built communities and resisted slavery, from Frederick Douglass's writing to Nat Turner's rebellion (1831). A distinct American culture emerged in literature (the transcendentalists) and art.
points: Reform grew from religious revival and democratic ideals.
Expanding democracy was limited by race and sex.

example.prompt: Explain one cause of the expansion of slavery in the early 1800s.
example.solution: The cotton gin made short-staple cotton profitable to grow inland, and rising demand from British and Northern textile mills made cotton planting extremely profitable, so planters expanded slavery into new lands in the Deep South.

misconceptions: It expanded voting mainly for white men.
Worcester v. Georgia ruled for the Cherokee, but Jackson's administration carried out removal anyway.
“The Market Revolution affected only the North.”
It tied Southern cotton to Northern and British industry.
Reform took many forms, and abolitionists were a minority even among reformers.

passages.title: Source A: William Lloyd Garrison, The Liberator, first issue, 1831
text: “I am aware that many object to the severity of my language; but is there not cause for severity? I will be as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice. On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation. No! No! Tell a man whose house is on fire to give a moderate alarm . . . but urge me not to use moderation in a cause like the present. I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD.”
passages.attribution: William Lloyd Garrison, “To the Public,” in the first issue of his abolitionist newspaper The Liberator, Boston, January 1, 1831. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 13.4.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/13-4-addressing-slavery); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Chief Justice John Marshall, Worcester v. Georgia, 1832
text: “The Cherokee Nation, then, is a distinct community, occupying its own territory, with boundaries accurately described, in which the laws of Georgia can have no force, and which the citizens of Georgia have no right to enter but with the assent of the Cherokees themselves or in conformity with treaties and with the acts of Congress. The whole intercourse between the United States and this nation is, by our Constitution and laws, vested in the government of the United States. . . . The Acts of Georgia are repugnant to the Constitution, laws, and treaties of the United States.”
passages.attribution: Chief Justice John Marshall, majority opinion of the U.S. Supreme Court in Worcester v. Georgia, 1832. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 10.4.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/10-4-indian-removal); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of the Market Revolution
text: “Between 1815 and 1848, Americans increasingly produced not for their own households but for distant markets. The Erie Canal cut the cost of shipping goods from the Great Lakes to New York City dramatically, and farmers in Ohio began growing wheat for buyers they would never meet. In New England, young women left family farms to tend power looms in Lowell's mills, earning wages of their own. In the South, cotton grown by enslaved people fed those same looms. The new economy tied the regions together even as it made them more different from one another.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of Jacksonian democracy
text: “The age of Andrew Jackson is often called an age of the common man, and for many white men it was. Property requirements for voting disappeared in most states, party conventions replaced closed caucuses, and turnout in presidential elections rose sharply. But the same years saw free Black men lose the right to vote in several states, women remain excluded, and the forced removal of the Cherokee and other Southeastern nations. Democracy expanded for some by drawing its boundaries more sharply around others.”

questions.prompt: Garrison's main purpose in the excerpt is to
choices: support the colonization of freed people in Africa
call for compromise with slaveholders
argue for gradually ending slavery over many decades
defend his uncompromising language against slavery
questions.explanation: He insists he will not use moderation and will not retreat: he demands immediate action.
choiceExplanations: He had turned against colonization schemes.
He says he will not compromise.
He rejects moderation and gradualism.

Populism came in the 1890s.

questions.prompt: Which development was a direct response to the kind of abolitionist activism reflected in the excerpt?
choices: The Missouri Compromise was repealed
The Supreme Court decided Worcester v. Georgia
The House of Representatives adopted a “gag rule” to table antislavery petitions
Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: From 1836 to 1844 the House automatically tabled antislavery petitions, a defensive response by Southern members and their allies.
choiceExplanations: The Missouri Compromise was effectively repealed in 1854, for other reasons.
Worcester concerned Cherokee sovereignty.
The Thirteenth Amendment came in 1865.

choices: more moderate, because he accepted slavery's continuation
more radical, because he demanded immediate emancipation
identical in its goals and methods
focused mainly on ending the slave trade with Africa
questions.explanation: Garrison's call for immediate, uncompromising abolition marked a sharper break than gradual approaches.
choiceExplanations: He rejected compromise.
His demand for immediacy was new.
The Atlantic slave trade had already been banned in 1808; he targeted slavery itself.

the Cherokee must move west of the Mississippi

He rules the opposite.

choices: The Jackson administration pursued removal anyway, leading to the Trail of Tears
Georgia returned all Cherokee lands
Congress repealed the Indian Removal Act
The Cherokee were granted U.S. citizenship and statehood
questions.explanation: Despite the ruling, the federal government enforced removal, and thousands of Cherokee died on the forced march of 1838–1839.
choiceExplanations: Georgia continued to take Cherokee land.
The Removal Act stayed in force.
No such outcome occurred.

The opening of the Erie Canal
The expansion of cotton cultivation and the discovery of gold on Cherokee lands
The growth of textile mills in Lowell
questions.explanation: Settlers wanted Cherokee lands for cotton, and the 1829 gold rush in north Georgia intensified demands.
choiceExplanations: This doesn't explain demand for Cherokee land.
The canal affected New York and the Great Lakes.
Mills created demand for cotton but were far away.

It forced them to stop farming
It closed markets in New York City
It required them to grow cotton
questions.explanation: Cheaper shipping connected Western farms to Eastern markets.

It opened, not closed, those markets.
Cotton was grown in the South.

The end of women's work

The Monroe Doctrine
The Indian Removal Act
The Wilmot Proviso
questions.explanation: The American System sought federally supported roads and canals to strengthen the national market.
choiceExplanations: The Monroe Doctrine concerned European colonization in the Western Hemisphere.
Removal concerned American Indian lands.
The Wilmot Proviso came in 1846 and concerned slavery.
